transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-08
Start: 10:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Carlos (CSM) -- Lena, Arjun, Priya, Noah (Quantaco)
Links referenced: pricing spreadsheet (redwood.com/pricing/DEAL-78291), benchmark logs (shared link), security deck (s3 link)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll keep to 45 minutes. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Lena: Lena here.
[00:10] Arjun: Arjun, hi.
[00:12] Priya: Priya, thanks.
[00:14] Noah: Noah.
[00:16] Ethan: Ethan from Redwood SE.
[00:18] Maya: Great, Carlos is on for notes. Today we want to review the cost/unit economics from last week's runs, caching and batching tradeoffs, and agree next steps.

[00:45] Ethan: Quick recap — we ran three configurations last 48 hours: hosted baseline (our standard hosted API), dedicated GPU pool with conservative batching, and dedicated with aggressive batching + prefix caching enabled. The metrics we focused on were tokens/sec and tokens per dollar (tokens/$), plus tail latencies.

[01:20] Lena: Can you remind us what model variant you used for dedicated? Was it the 70B quantized variant?
[01:24] Ethan: Yes, we used the 70B-4q quantized variant that we onboarded, which is labelled in the deck as "rwd-70b-q4" — sometimes transcripts show it wrong as "rwd70 q four" but that's the one.

[01:45] Maya: Also note the dedicated pool had a KV cache warmup script we primed with the 5k most common prefixes from your sample traffic. That drastically affected the cost numbers once cache warmed.

[02:15] Arjun: We observed a big delta in tokens/sec when the cache hit rate rose, yes. Can you quantify the savings?
[02:22] Ethan: Sure, initial cold runs showed ~1,100 tokens/sec on dedicated with conservative batching, tokens/$ about 18k tokens per dollar. After prefix cache warmed to ~62% hit rate, effective tokens/sec jumped to ~1,800 and tokens/$ improved to ~28k. With aggressive batching + cache hit ~68% we saw peak tokens/sec ~2,300 but 95th percentile latency rose from ~160ms to ~320ms.

[03:05] Priya: So caching looks huge for cost; but worried about that latency bump with aggressive batching — our product needs snappy responses for interactive flows.

[03:14] Ethan: Right, that's the tradeoff. Batching increases throughput and reduces cost per token but it introduces queueing latency. For interactive routes we recommend smaller batch windows and rely more on KV caching. For background/async workloads we can push aggressive batching.

[03:45] Lena: Do you have exact cost estimates for hybrid approach — interactive via hosted, background via dedicated?
[03:50] Maya: We put together a pricing scenario: hosted for interactive with estimated tokens/sec lower but lower latency SLO, and dedicated for batch expensive jobs. On your sample traffic (avg 1.2M tokens/day, 5% interactive), the blended tokens/$ came out to ~23k tokens per dollar and overall monthly cost was ~$12.4k with a small reserved commit. I'll send the spreadsheet after the call.

[04:20] Noah: Is the tokens/$ metric normalized across model variants? If Quantaco chooses a smaller model for some routes, how do numbers change?
[04:26] Ethan: Good question — tokens/$ is model-dependent. For a 13B quantized variant we typically see 2.5x tokens/$ compared to 70B because FLOP/cost is lower, but quality differs. We can give you per-route guidance — map route labels to model choices in the spreadsheet.

[05:05] Arjun: About the prefix cache: you mentioned we primed with top 5k prefixes. For production, what sizes and eviction strategy do you recommend?
[05:12] Ethan: Based on your distribution, a 10k prefix cache with LRU eviction and periodic refresh of top prefixes every 6 hours hits a sweet spot. If your hotset is small, you get >70% hit rate. If it's broader, we can use adaptive policies which Redwood runtime supports — it will keep the cache focused on the most recent high-frequency prefixes.

[05:50] Priya: Any security concerns with caching — are cached KV entries encrypted at rest?
[05:55] Carlos: Quick pickup — yes, for dedicated/private we encrypt KV cache at rest using customer's KMS when configured; in hosted we manage KMS but can use customer-managed keys for enterprise tier. We'll link the security doc.

[06:20] Lena: Back to latency: you said 95th went to 320ms with aggressive batching; what's P99?
[06:26] Ethan: P99 was closer to 540ms in those runs. Those were synthetic high-concurrency spike tests. In steady-state, with adaptive batching we saw P99 ~380ms.

[06:50] Lena: For our UI, P99 above 400ms could be noticeable. I think we need to keep interactive routes below that.

[07:05] Maya: Agreed. So recommendation: interactive routes pinned to hosted or dedicated with batch window <= 10ms and caching prioritized; background pipelines with batch window 50-100ms to maximize throughput.

[07:30] Arjun: What about autoscaling behavior for dedicated? If we get a sudden spike are we protected or will requests queue and latency spike?
[07:38] Ethan: Dedicated pool autoscaling has a short provisioning time; we also support burst capacity — think of a two-tier fallback: immediate burst into smaller reserved instances + routing to hosted as a failover. That reduces queuing risk. We'll add concrete numbers in the follow-up doc.

[08:05] Noah: Can we talk about sample-run logs you shared? I saw an odd line where it reported "KV cash" in the logs — possible transcriptiontypo?
[08:12] Ethan: Yeah, that's a minor log artifact — some of our older tools write it that way in debug, but product code uses "KV cache". Noted.

[08:40] Maya: Let's walk the benchmark timeline briefly — early morning run (low conc) vs afternoon spike. Ethan, can you narrate the key segments?
[08:47] Ethan: Early morning low conc: cache hit ~30% because fewer repeated prefixes, tokens/sec ~900. Afternoon spike: hit climbed to 62% as repeated queries arrived, tokens/sec peaked 2.1k on dedicated with moderate batching. Costs scaled sublinearly because cache hits avoid full decoding for prefix.

[09:20] Priya: Do you expose the micro-metrics so we can plot tokens/sec/$ per route?
[09:24] Ethan: Yes, Redwood Console provides per-route token counts, cost breakout and trace hooks. We'll share a dashboard link.

[09:35] Lena: On pricing, if we move to a reserved commit for dedicated, what's the discount ladder?
[09:39] Maya: Typical discounts scale with commit size and term. For a 12-month commit at your expected usage we can offer 15% off host-equivalent unit cost; larger commits or multi-year get deeper. I'll include scenario lines in the pricing sheet.

[10:05] Arjun: Quick technical: does the runtime co-locate KV cache with GPU memory or is it on host?
[10:10] Ethan: The KV cache is kept in GPU-friendly memory structures; depending on quantization and model size we keep hot KV segments on device to avoid PCIe hops. Some metadata lives on host. That’s why cache hit latency is low.

[10:35] Noah: For our compliance team, can you provide audit logs of who accessed what cache/key?
[10:40] Carlos: Yes — we produce audit trails with SSO identities; for private deployments we can store logs in your S3 bucket and rotate per your policy.

[11:00] Priya: A practical question — we saw some prompts that warmed the cache but then later had slightly different prefixes so hit rate dropped. Any suggestions to stabilize?
[11:08] Ethan: Two approaches: normalize prompts client-side (strip user IDs, canonicalize punctuation) or use approximate prefix matching in the cache layer. We can prototype both. Normalization often yields the biggest win.

[11:35] Lena: For the tokens/$ numbers, is cost per token dominated by GPU runtime or by other infra (network, storage)?
[11:41] Ethan: Dominated by GPU cycles; network and storage are minor. So model size and quantization are the primary levers. Also batching efficiency affects GPU utilization and thus cost.

[12:05] Maya: Let's talk about a concrete pilot goal: show a 2x improvement in tokens/$ for background pipelines while keeping interactive P99 under 400ms. Can we commit to that as success criteria?

[12:15] Lena: Yes that sounds reasonable. We'll measure over a two-week window.

[12:25] Arjun: And define measurement method — do we use Redwood's Console numbers as single source?

[12:30] Maya: Yes, Redwood Console plus exported logs. We'll agree a start date when Quantaco provides daily traffic files.

[12:48] Noah: When can we start the two-week measurement? Assuming next week we finalize reserved config.

[12:53] Maya: If you confirm token budget and spike windows by Monday (2026-07-13) we can start a baseline run Wednesday and kickoff measurement Friday — timeline in the next steps doc.

[13:10] Priya: Any risk with burst routing to hosted during spikes — does that change data residency?

[13:16] Carlos: It can if hosted region differs; we can restrict fallback to same-region hosted endpoints or force regional routing. We'll document options.

[13:38] Ethan: Small note: during dedicated GPU runs we observed occasional GC pauses in a helper service that briefly affected throughput; we patched and re-ran. We'll share the fixed benchmark.

[14:05] Lena: Ok, can you summarise the three recommended configs and expected tokens/$ and latencies?

[14:10] Ethan: Sure — (1) Hosted interactive: tokens/$ ~15k, P95 ~120ms, P99 ~220ms. (2) Dedicated interactive (small batch): tokens/$ ~22k, P95 ~180ms, P99 ~360ms. (3) Dedicated batch (aggressive): tokens/$ ~30k, P95 ~320ms, P99 ~540ms. These are approximate and depend on final cache hit and model mix.

[15:00] Priya: That helps. For route mapping, we'll send a list of three example routes and expected SLA.

[15:10] Maya: Great — we'll annotate the spreadsheet with where each route fits.

[15:28] Carlos: Action recap: Ethan runs 24h benchmark (due 7/15), Maya sends pricing/reserved scenarios (due 7/10), Quantaco confirms token budget (due 7/13), Noah to share hotset (due 7/12).

[15:45] Lena: One last question — any suggested quantization profile changes that might help cost without quality regressions?

[15:52] Ethan: We can test a mixed precision profile: keep attention & layernorm in fp16 and most weights in 4-bit. In our internal evals that often preserves quality but yields 20-30% improvement in tokens/$. We'll run a small eval set.

[16:15] Priya: Sounds good.

[16:18] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the spreadsheet, dashboard and benchmark logs. Meeting closed.

Notes: transcript contains occasional transcription artifacts (e.g., "KV cash", mis-typed model tags), filler words and interruptions preserved.
